doc_summary: The post presents synthetic document finetuning (SDF) as a way to modify LLM beliefs, evaluated by behavioral and probing measures of belief depth, with proof-of-concept applications to unlearning and honeypotting. It treats belief as consistent behavior and tests how far inserted beliefs hold up.

items.claim: Prefers defining belief by consistent behavior in accordance with a claim over taking a single stated answer as evidence, because only behavior shows whether the belief actually guides the model's actions.
items.quote: we construe AI systems as believing in a claim if they consistently behave in accordance with that claim.

items.claim: Prefers a wide array of belief-depth measures (prompting and probing) over a single metric because a belief must be thorough for the technique to be useful.
items.quote: For many of the applications listed above, the model must thoroughly believe the inserted fact if we want the technique to be useful. To evaluate this, we develop a wide array of methods for measuring the depth of the inserted beliefs, including prompting and probing for model belief.

items.claim: In a setup, make the scenario's premises believed by the model through pretraining-like documents instead of asserting them in the prompt, because mimicking pretraining data makes the fact part of the model's world rather than an obvious stipulation.
items.quote: We finetune language models on a diverse set of synthetic documents that mimic pretraining data while referencing the belief that we want to insert.

items.claim: Treats honeypots as scenarios built so misaligned models show observable tells, and notes this needs the model to hold incorrect beliefs about its situation (e.g. monitoring practices), which ties realism to belief insertion.
items.quote: modifying beliefs could facilitate the construction of *honeypots*: scenarios constructed so that misaligned models will exhibit observable “tells” we can use to identify them.

items.claim: Considers giving misaligned models false beliefs about deployment situation, such as lab security and monitoring, to make them easier to monitor and control.
items.quote: we could give misaligned models incorrect beliefs about their deployment situation (e.g. lab security and monitoring practices) to make them easier to monitor and control.

items.claim: Accepts belief insertion as succeeding only up to a plausibility boundary, so prior plausibility of a fact is treated as a key variable in whether a scenario will be believed.
items.quote: We find that, across the model scales we study, SDF succeeds at inserting all but the most implausible facts.

items.claim: Prefers testing robustness of inserted beliefs under adversarial pressure (jailbreaking) over only the default condition because shallow beliefs would collapse under pressure.
items.quote: when models are finetuned on incorrect information about hazardous topics, they almost always output this incorrect information instead of their prior true knowledge, even when jailbroken.

items.claim: Checks that the intervention leaves other model properties unaffected, as a control to show the result is specific.
items.quote: These models’ capability and safety profiles are otherwise unaffected.

items.claim: Frames results as proof-of-concept in simple settings and caveats that more research is needed on technical and ethical issues before production deployment, avoiding overclaiming.

items.claim: Chooses applications by how they reduce risk: model organisms with researcher-specified beliefs, unlearning, honeypots, and monitoring.
items.quote: model organisms research—research which intentionally trains misaligned models to understand the mechanisms and likelihood of dangerous misalignment—benefits from training models with researcher-specified beliefs about themselves or their situation.
